questions.question: Fixed resistor 1.20 k ohm in series with LDR across 12.0 V (negligible internal resistance). Voltmeter across LDR reads 4.71 V in dark and 2.16 V in light. Find the change in LDR resistance.
questions.answer: Change in resistance = -512 ohm (about 510 ohm decrease)
steps: Fixed resistor and LDR are in series, so their p.d.s add to 12.0 V.
Dark: p.d. across fixed resistor = 12.0 - 4.71 = 7.29 V.
Current (same through both) I = 7.29 / 1200 = 6.08 x 10^-3 A.
Dark LDR resistance = 4.71 / 6.08 x 10^-3 = 775 ohm.
Light: p.d. across fixed resistor = 12.0 - 2.16 = 9.84 V; I = 9.84 / 1200 = 8.20 x 10^-3 A.
Light LDR resistance = 2.16 / 8.20 x 10^-3 = 263 ohm.
Change = 263 - 775 = -512 ohm, so the resistance falls by about 510 ohm.

questions.question: Two resistors each of resistance R are connected to a battery of e.m.f. E and internal resistance r, first in series (A) then in parallel (B). Which arrangement gives the greater terminal p.d.?
questions.answer: Series arrangement A gives the greater terminal p.d.
steps: Terminal p.d. V = E x R_ext / (R_ext + r), where R_ext is the external resistance.
Series: R_ext = 2R, so V_A = 2RE / (2R + r).
Parallel: R_ext = R/2, so V_B = (R/2)E / (R/2 + r) = RE / (R + 2r).
Ratio V_A / V_B = 2(R + 2r) / (2R + r) = (2R + 4r) / (2R + r), which is greater than 1 because 4r > r.
So V_A > V_B: the series arrangement gives the greater terminal p.d. (more external resistance means less lost to internal resistance).

questions.question: Which of the following is an SI unit for e.m.f.? A coulomb, B joule, C newton, D volt.

questions.question: Cell of e.m.f. E and internal resistance r supplies current I with terminal p.d. V. Which expression gives the power dissipated in the internal resistance? A P = I(E - V), B P = I^2 R, C P = I..., D P = V^2/r.
questions.answer: A, P = I(E - V)
steps: Power in internal resistance P = I^2 r.
Lost p.d. inside the cell is Ir = E - V (E is split between external and internal parts).
So P = I x Ir = I(E - V), which is option A.
Option B uses R (external resistance), so it is not the internal power.

questions.question: Which graph shows how power P dissipated by an ohmic conductor varies with p.d. V across it?

questions.question: Derive an equation for the combined resistance RT of two resistors R1 and R2 in series.
questions.answer: RT = R1 + R2
steps: In series the same current I flows through both resistors.
Total p.d. is the sum of the p.d.s: V = V1 + V2.
Using V = IR: I RT = I R1 + I R2.
Divide by I: RT = R1 + R2.

questions.question: Explain why the power in the fixed resistor decreases as light intensity on an LDR decreases, referring to electrons in the LDR.
questions.answer: Lower light gives fewer electrons promoted to the conduction band, so the LDR resistance rises, the current falls and P = I^2 R in the fixed resistor decreases.
steps: Lower light intensity means fewer photons, so fewer electrons are excited into the conduction band.
Fewer charge carriers (free electrons) means the LDR resistance increases.
Total resistance in the series circuit increases, so the current I = E / R_total decreases.
Power in the fixed resistor P = I^2 R decreases because I has decreased (R is constant).

questions.question: Potential divider with battery (negligible internal resistance) and LDR; voltmeter across fixed resistor. Which statement is correct? A LDR resistance halves so reading halves; B increasing light decreases reading; C increasing light has no effect; D reading plus LDR p.d. always equals 12.0 V.
questions.answer: D
steps: Fixed resistor and LDR are in series across the battery, so their p.d.s always sum to the e.m.f. (12.0 V).
A is wrong: the p.d. does not simply halve when R halves (it depends on the ratio of resistances).
B is wrong: more light lowers LDR resistance, so the p.d. across the fixed resistor increases.
C is wrong: light intensity changes the reading.
D is correct by the series voltage rule.

questions.answer: E.m.f. is the energy transferred per unit charge by the source (from chemical to electrical energy) in driving charge round the whole circuit.

Equivalently, it is the total energy per coulomb supplied by the cell, including energy lost inside it.

questions.question: Car battery emf 12.00 V. Voltmeter reads 11.81 V and ammeter reads 9.83 A. Calculate the internal resistance.
questions.answer: r = 0.019 ohm (about 0.0193 ohm)
steps: Lost p.d. inside the battery = E - V = 12.00 - 11.81 = 0.19 V.
Ohm's law for internal resistance: r = (E - V) / I = 0.19 / 9.83.
r = 0.0193 ohm, about 0.019 ohm.

questions.question: Describe how readings of ammeter and voltmeter from several resistor settings can be used graphically to find internal resistance.
questions.answer: Plot V (y) against I (x); the gradient magnitude gives r and the y-intercept gives E.
steps: Adjust the variable resistor and record V and I for several settings.
Plot a graph of terminal p.d. V against current I (V on the y-axis).
The equation V = E - Ir is a straight line with gradient -r.
Find the gradient of the best-fit line and take its magnitude: this is the internal resistance r.
The y-intercept (current = 0) gives the e.m.f. E.

questions.question: A 9.0 V cell with internal resistance 0.10 ohm supplies a 5.0 ohm resistor. The student claims that when r rises to 0.50 ohm, the power in the resistor falls to 70% of original. Is this correct?

steps: Ratio = 13.4 / 15.6 = 0.86, so the power is about 86% of its original value.
86% is not 70%, so the student's conclusion is incorrect.

questions.question: A lightning strike 1 km away gives a 3 s delay before thunder. Speed of sound is 340 m/s. Determine whether the teacher is correct.
questions.answer: Approximately correct: the delay is about 2.9 s, which rounds to 3 s.
steps: Time t = distance / speed = 1000 / 340.
t = 2.94 s, which is about 3 s to one significant figure.
The teacher is essentially correct; the light arrives almost instantly so the delay is due only to the sound.

questions.question: Show that the resistivity of air in the lightning channel is about 0.2 ohm m, using distance 400 m, current 25 000 A, p.d. 1.2 x 10^9 V and diameter 5.0 cm.
questions.answer: Resistivity = 0.24 ohm m, which is about 0.2 ohm m.
steps: Resistance R = V / I = 1.2 x 10^9 / 2.5 x 10^4 = 4.8 x 10^4 ohm.
Cross-sectional area A = pi r^2 with r = 0.025 m: A = 1.96 x 10^-3 m^2.
Resistivity rho = R A / L = (4.8 x 10^4 x 1.96 x 10^-3) / 400.
rho = 94.2 / 400 = 0.24 ohm m, about 0.2 ohm m as required.

questions.question: The accepted resistivity of air is 10^16 ohm m. Suggest why the value calculated from the data is much smaller.
questions.answer: The lightning heats and ionises the air in the channel, creating many free charge carriers, so it conducts far better than normal air.
steps: Normal air is an almost perfect insulator, so its resistivity is very high.
The strike ionises the air in the channel, producing many free electrons and ions.
More charge carriers means much lower resistivity, so the calculated value is far smaller.

questions.question: Explain the process by which nitrogen atoms produce a line spectrum.
questions.answer: Electrons are excited to higher energy levels by collisions and then fall back, emitting photons of discrete frequencies.
steps: Energy from the lightning strike (collisions) excites electrons in nitrogen atoms to higher energy levels.
Electrons then fall back to lower energy levels (de-excitation).
Each fall releases a photon with energy equal to the energy difference, E = hf.
Because the energy levels are discrete, only certain frequencies are emitted, giving a line spectrum.

questions.question: State why the line spectrum from oxygen atoms would differ from that of nitrogen atoms.
questions.answer: Oxygen and nitrogen atoms have different energy level structures, so their emitted photon energies (frequencies) differ.
steps: Each element has its own set of electron energy levels.
So the energy differences between levels, and hence photon frequencies, differ for each element.

Power is derived (energy divided by time), so B is correct.

questions.question: Explain, in terms of particles, why the resistance of a filament lamp increases as the p.d. across it increases.
questions.answer: Higher p.d. gives higher current and more energy in the filament, so the metal ions vibrate more and collisions with electrons increase, raising resistance.
steps: Greater p.d. drives more current through the filament.
Greater current means more energy is transferred to the filament, so it heats up.
The metal ions in the lattice vibrate with greater amplitude.
Electrons collide more frequently with the vibrating ions, reducing their drift velocity for a given field, so resistance increases.

questions.question: Assess whether doubling the e.m.f. of the battery will double the voltmeter reading.
questions.answer: Correct: with negligible internal resistance, every p.d. in the circuit is proportional to the e.m.f., so doubling it doubles the voltmeter reading (provided the thermistor resistance is unchanged).
steps: The battery has negligible internal resistance, so the full e.m.f. appears across the external circuit.
The current I = E / R_total is proportional to E for a fixed total resistance.
Each p.d. V = IR is therefore proportional to E.
Doubling E doubles the current and the voltmeter reading, so the student is correct, as long as the thermistor temperature (and resistance) does not change.

questions.question: Explain how the counterweight affects the work required from the motor to raise the lift.
questions.answer: The counterweight balances part of the lift's weight, so the motor does less work to raise the lift.
steps: The counterweight's weight acts in the opposite direction to the lift's weight.

questions.question: The motor raises the lift 40.0 m in 30.0 s. Lift and people 2250 kg, counterweight 1300 kg. Show that the output power is about 12 kW.

steps: Input power = useful output power + wasted power = 12.4 kW + 3.6 kW = 16.0 kW.

questions.question: Explain why there is a maximum current that can be supplied by the battery.
questions.answer: The maximum current occurs when the external resistance is zero (short circuit): I = E / r, limited only by the internal resistance.
steps: Current I = E / (R + r).
As the external resistance R falls towards zero, the current rises.
It cannot exceed E / r because the internal resistance r always limits it.

questions.question: Copper wires connect nichrome wire to a cell; wires have the same diameter; copper has more conduction electrons per m^3. Compare the average electron velocity in the copper and nichrome.
questions.answer: The electrons in the copper wires have a lower average (drift) velocity than in the nichrome wire, since the current is the same and copper has a higher carrier density.
steps: The copper and nichrome are in series, so the current I is the same in both.
Drift velocity v = I / (n A e), with the same area A for both wires (same diameter).
Copper has a greater n, so v is smaller in copper.
Hence the electrons in the copper move more slowly than in the nichrome.

questions.question: State what is meant by the resistivity of a material.
questions.answer: Resistivity is the resistance of a sample of unit length and unit cross-sectional area of the material (rho = R A / L).
steps: Resistivity is a property of the material, independent of its size.
It is the resistance of a 1 m length with a 1 m^2 cross-sectional area, rho = RA / L.

questions.question: Describe how the student could determine the resistivity of the conducting material from a sample.
questions.answer: Measure resistance R by V/I, measure length L and cross-sectional area A, then rho = RA/L; repeat and average.
steps: Measure the length L of the sample with a ruler and its width and thickness (or diameter) to find A.
Connect the sample to a cell, ammeter and voltmeter and measure V and I to find R = V / I.
Calculate resistivity rho = R A / L.
Repeat for several readings and average to reduce random error.

questions.topic: Copper Low Resistivity and Drift Velocity
questions.question: Explain how the low resistivity of copper affects the drift velocity of electrons in the copper electrodes.
questions.answer: Copper has a high density of conduction electrons, so for the same current the drift velocity of electrons in the copper is low.
steps: Low resistivity means copper has a very high number density of charge carriers n.
Drift velocity v = I / (n A e), so for a given current v is small when n is large.
So electrons in the copper electrodes drift slowly, and the electrodes carry current with little heating.

questions.question: Explain how adding panels in parallel changes the power output of the heating system.
questions.answer: Adding panels in parallel lowers the total resistance, so more current is drawn and the power output increases.
steps: Panels in parallel: total resistance falls as more branches are added.
For a fixed supply p.d. V, the power output P = V^2 / R_total increases.
So the power output increases.

questions.answer: E = 5 sqrt(P R)
steps: Power in resistor P = I^2 R, so I = sqrt(P / R).
Total resistance = 4R + R = 5R, so E = I x 5R.
Substitute: E = 5R sqrt(P / R) = 5 sqrt(P R).

questions.question: Describe the photoelectric effect.
questions.answer: Electrons are emitted from a metal surface when electromagnetic radiation of sufficiently high frequency is incident on it.
steps: Electromagnetic radiation incident on a metal surface transfers energy to electrons, one photon per electron.
If the photon frequency is above the threshold frequency, electrons are emitted immediately.
Emission depends on frequency, not on intensity.

questions.question: Explain why the photomultiplier cannot detect some frequencies of electromagnetic radiation.
questions.answer: Photons below the threshold frequency have energy hf less than the work function, so they cannot release electrons.
steps: Photon energy E = hf.
If hf is less than the work function of the photocathode, no electron is emitted.
So low-frequency radiation is not detected.

questions.question: Visible light spans 380 nm to 700 nm; the photocathode work function is 1.48 eV. Deduce whether the photomultiplier detects all visible wavelengths.
questions.answer: Yes: the threshold wavelength is about 840 nm, which is longer than 700 nm, so all visible light releases electrons.
steps: Threshold wavelength: lambda = hc / phi = 1240 eV nm / 1.48 eV = 838 nm.
Light is detected only if its wavelength is shorter than the threshold, i.e. below about 838 nm.
The longest visible wavelength is 700 nm, which is less than 838 nm, so all visible wavelengths are detected.

questions.question: An electron leaves the photocathode at 1.35 x 10^6 m s^-1, with p.d. 108 V to the first plate. Calculate its kinetic energy when it hits the plate.

questions.topic: Removing Layer Effect on Electron Release Rate
questions.question: Layer 1 (greater work function than layer 2) is removed so all photons reach layer 2. Explain how this affects the rate at which electrons are released, assuming each layer absorbs all photons above its threshold frequency.
questions.answer: The rate of electron release is unchanged: all photons above layer 2's threshold are absorbed in either case, so the same number of electrons is released per second, just now only from layer 2.
steps: With layer 1 present, photons above f1 are absorbed by layer 1; photons between f2 and f1 pass on and are absorbed by layer 2.
Without layer 1, all photons above f2 reach and are absorbed by layer 2.
Intensity is constant, so the number of photons absorbed per second (and so electrons released per second) is the same.
Only the location of emission changes; the rate is unchanged.

questions.question: Two solar cells each with e.m.f. 5.0 V and internal resistance 0.80 ohm drive a 4.0 ohm resistor. Series gives 13 W. Deduce whether parallel connection gives less than half this power.

questions.topic: LDR Light Effect on Terminal PD
questions.question: The voltmeter measures the terminal p.d. of a cell in series with an LDR. Explain how increasing light intensity on the LDR affects the voltmeter reading.

questions.question: Explain why the battery gets hot when the e-bike goes up a steep hill.
questions.answer: Climbing a steep hill needs more power from the motor, so the battery supplies a larger current; the power wasted in its internal resistance (I^2 r) rises, and this is dissipated as heat.
steps: Going up a steep hill requires more work against gravity, so the motor needs more power.
The battery supplies more power, so the current drawn from it increases.
Power dissipated as heat in the battery's internal resistance is P = I^2 r.
Since I is larger, the power wasted as heat increases sharply, so the battery warms up.
